title: Photoelectron Spectroscopy
intro: A spectrometer shines light on a gas of atoms and catches the electrons that fly out. Today you read what those electrons say about the atom.
introSteps: Look at the unlabeled spectrum below. Then read three short cards: what a photoelectron is, what binding energy is, and what a peak is.
Walk to the spectrometer. Yellow arrows show each control the first time you need it.
Work the steps in order, Part A to Part E. Each step opens when the one before it is done.
At three checkpoints you answer a fresh question each time. Three right in a row passes. If you are stuck, press I need Mr. D.
Your written answers go on the paper worksheet. The lab keeps a record on this computer for Mr. D.
keyRows: Walk. On screen you move along the floor diagonals.
Use what you are facing (the spectrometer).
Point at anything to see its name.

hook.note: Each bar is a group of electrons. By the end of the lab you can read it.

goal: Goal: read each peak as a measure of how hard some electrons are held, and match a spectrum to an element.

cards.body: Light carries energy. When a beam of light hits an atom with enough energy, it can knock an electron out of the atom. The electron that flies out is a photoelectron. It leaves with the energy that is left over after it breaks free.

Binding energy is how hard an electron is to knock loose. A big number means the electron is held tightly. A small number means it comes loose easily. Light that is too weak for an electron frees nothing at all, however bright it is.

The spectrometer counts the electrons it catches and sorts them by how hard they were held. Electrons held equally hard land together and make one tall bar, called a peak. The place of the peak shows how hard they were held. The height shows how many electrons there are.

reading: Bottom: how hard the electrons are held, in MJ/mol. Big numbers are on the left and small numbers on the right. Each step is ten times the last, because the innermost electrons are held so hard they would fall off a normal page. Side: how many electrons.
One peak is one group of electrons held equally hard. Its place is how hard. Its height is how many.
Find the peak farthest left: the hardest to knock loose. Then count the peaks from left to right. Then read each height.

model.A: Model A: all electrons in the same shell are held equally hard, so each shell gives one peak.

model.after: Your choice is saved. Write your reason on the paper worksheet.

demo: Welcome. This tour shows every control. None of it counts toward your lab.
Walk with the arrow keys or WASD. Press E at the spectrometer, the long machine in the middle of the room.
The carousel holds one gas for each element. Click a cell to load that gas.
The light color dial sets how much energy each photon carries. Most visible light is too weak to free any electron.
Fire sends light in. Brightness only sets how fast counts build. It never changes which peaks appear.
Electrons that fly out are counted and sorted by how hard they were held. A spectrum builds. Click a peak to see its subshell, its electrons and its energy.
The zoom view shows the atom, a photon hitting it, and an electron leaving. Its speed comes from the energy left over.
At a checkpoint you answer a fresh question each time. Three right in a row passes.
Three misses in a row, or I need Mr. D, locks the screen. Mr. D types a PIN to unlock it.
That is the tour. In the lab, yellow arrows will walk you through each step.
